name: Aappudaiyar Temple, Tiruappanur
deity: Shiva as Aappudaiyar (Aappanathar), with the goddess Kuzhalvaimozhi Ammai
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Pandya country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); Pandya foundation with later Nayak additions
dynasty: Pandya, with later Madurai Nayak patronage
summary: Aappudaiyar is the Shiva temple on the north bank of the Vaigai at Sellur in Madurai, sung by Tirugnana Sambandar in the Tevaram and remembered for the legend of the aappu, the wedge that became a linga to help a Pandya king cross the flooded river.

sections.history: Tiruappanur lies in Sellur, on the northern bank of the Vaigai, a few kilometres from the great Meenakshi temple of Madurai. Tradition counts it the second of the Tevaram shrines of the Pandya country praised in the hymns of Tirugnana Sambandar, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The original temple is believed to have been raised by the Pandyas and later enlarged by the Nayak rulers of Madurai. The name of the place is explained by the story of the aappu, and the river that flows beside the shrine has long been honoured as its sacred water. Though the city has grown all around it, worship here has continued without a break. Detailed records of its foundation are scarce, so this account keeps to what tradition holds.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and is modest in scale beside the great monuments of old Madurai. Its plan follows the Somaskanda arrangement, with a shrine of Subrahmanya standing between the sanctum of Aappudaiyar and that of the goddess, and a Vinayaka beneath a sacred fig between them. The sanctum holds the Shiva linga, while Kuzhalvaimozhi Ammai is honoured in a shrine of her own. Accounts note that the Shiva sanctum has no towering gopuram of its own, and the Vaigai itself serves as the temple's sacred water. The sacred tree is the kondrai, the golden shower.
sections.legends: The temple takes its name from the aappu, the wedge. A Pandya king, called Solandhagan in some tellings, set out to worship at the Meenakshi temple but found the Vaigai in flood and could not cross. A wedge lying on the bank is said to have become a Shiva linga and shown him the way, and so the Lord is honoured here as Aappudaiyar. Another telling remembers him as Annavinodhar, the Lord who in a time of famine turned river sand into rice. Both stories run on one thread, the compassion of a Lord who gives what is needed at the moment of need.
sections.festivals: On Panguni Uthiram, in March or April, the images of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar are brought across the river from the Madurai temple to Tiruappanur, a festival that binds the two sanctuaries together. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple, and the Tamil-month festivals of the Madurai region are kept here with devotion. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Come to the bank of the Vaigai from the bustle of Madurai and give this shrine an unhurried visit. Stand first before Aappudaiyar and recall the old story of the river that could not be crossed, then turn to Kuzhalvaimozhi Ammai in her own shrine. Bow to Vinayaka beneath the fig and to the shrine of Subrahmanya between the two sanctums, and sit for a while near the river. If you come on Panguni Uthiram, the meeting of the deities of the two great temples brings a particular fulfilment.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning (roughly 6:00 to 11:30) and again from late afternoon into the evening (roughly 4:30 to 8:00), with a midday break; listings vary, so confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruappanur is in Sellur, on the north bank of the Vaigai in Madurai, about 5 km from the Meenakshi temple. City buses 17, 17A and 17C from Periyar bus stand pass the temple; get down at the Tiruvaappudaiyar Kovil stop. The Simmakkal stop on the other side of the river is also close. Madurai Junction railway station and Madurai airport serve the city.
